description:
The shrine of Pir Lakha lies in the north-western uplands of the Jhal Magsi District of Balochistan, in the broken country near Kotra where the Moola river descends through its gorge — the same tract that holds the shrine of Pir Chhatal Shah Noorani (a separate entry in this dataset). District heritage listings count Pir Lakha among the principal shrines of Jhal Magsi, alongside the *dargahs* of Rakhyal Shah at Fatehpur and Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari at Gandava. Its particular fame rests less on a documented saintly biography — of which little is recorded — than on the hot springs beside it, known as *Aab-e-Shifa*, "the water of healing." Pilgrims travel from far-flung parts of Balochistan and Sindh to bathe in these thermal waters, which are believed to cure skin ailments and other afflictions, so that the site functions at once as a shrine and as a place of folk therapeutics. Like several shrines of the Kachhi–Gandava plain, it draws Muslim and Hindu visitors alike. Because the life of the eponymous *pir* is essentially undocumented in accessible sources, only the shrine's living role as a pilgrimage-and-healing centre can be stated with confidence. This listing is independently confirmed by the Jhal Magsi district government's own Culture & Heritage page, which names "Pir Lakha" both as a page heading and among the district's main shrines. That official listing, however, does not mention the Aab-e-Shifa hot springs at all; no citable source consulted for this entry corroborates the healing-spring claim that gives the site its popular name, which currently rests only on social-media and blog accounts.

## Bibliography

- "Culture & Heritage," Jhal Magsi District Government of Balochistan, archived 26 April 2025, http://web.archive.org/web/20250426101741/https://jhalmagsi.balochistan.gov.pk/culture-heritage/.
qa_note: The "Aab-e-Shifa" (healing-waters) claim that gives this shrine its popular name is not corroborated by any citable source found in the 2026-08 research pass. The one citable source verified — the Jhal Magsi district government's own Culture & Heritage page — confirms only that a shrine called "Pir Lakha" exists and is officially recognized as one of the district's main shrines; it does not mention hot springs, healing waters, or "Aab-e-Shifa" anywhere in its text. The hot-springs claim currently rests entirely on non-citable sources (Facebook posts and videos, tourism blogs, and an uncited line in Wikipedia's "Jhal Magsi" article). This addition rests on a single independently-verified source and has not yet been corroborated.
